CHAPTEB IV. 

AGRICULTURE AND FORESTS. 

The farm which was opened in 1897*08 has now^^P®”™®*: 
practically become a potato seed farm and in 1918 grew* 

OTer 1,000 mannds of seed for distribution. 

In connection with the cattle stock improvements it 
may be mentioned that of the stock imported in 1902 
and 1903, those which came from Patna have proved 
the better breed. Pure bred Patna bulls are being sold 
at the nominal rate of B-s. 60 each to Khasis for breed- 
ing purposes. Tho introduction of English and Austra- 
lian pigs in 1902 has proved a failure, but Dumba rams 
imported to improve sheep have proved a fair success.

The experimental fruit garden started in 1902 has 
not proved a success and the site was abandoned in 1902 
as a fruit garden and handed over to the Eoman 
Catholic Mission as a Scricultural farm, as it contains 
a largo number of mulberry trees. A new fruit garden 
on a more favourable site on the Jowai road was opened 
in 1913 and shows every sign of success. The tropical 
plantation opened in 1904i at Wahjain has not proved a 
success and was abandoned in 1911 as the site was

found ■anstiitable and tte soil too poor. Experimonts 
■were made with tea on the high plateau in 1904. At» 
tempts have also been made to introduce the oultiva'tion 
of silk. Seed of the univoltine worm was procured 
from Erance. and the experiment proved successful 
but the Elhasis do not seem inclined to take to sericul- 
ture. One or two individuals and the Koman Catholic 
Mission are however continuing the work and it is 
possible that in time the industry will spread.

The district forest administration was reorganised 
in 1907 with a separate office under the Deputy Com- 
missioner. The staff now consists of one Hanger, one 
Horester, one Head Guard and 14 permanent guards. 

Sleeper operations are carried on at Dmling near

CHAPTEH V. 

MISCELLANEOUS. 

Ccanmumoa* The Bilk Bungalows at Bumihat and Finsning 
(Naya Bungalow) were converted into Inspection 
Bungalows in 1912. At Nongpoh a cook and a khit- 
matgar are now maintained at the D0.k Bungalow and 
a tea house has recently been constructed by the road side

for the convenience of travellers. 

A daily service of motor-cars and lorries between 
Shillong, Gauhati and Pandughat has replaced the old 
tonga Service and connects up with the Eastern Bengal 
State Hailway. The journey from Shillong to Calcutta 
aud vice vend is now performed in a little over 24 hours. 

Shillong was constituted a station under Act V 
(B.O.) of 1876 in 1878 and afterwards converted into 
a Miudcipality' under Act III of 1884 in November 
1910. Its affairs are managed by a Committee of 16 
members presided over by the Deputy Commissioner. 
The principal sources of revenue are a tax on houses at 
7i per cent, of their annual rental, water and latrine 
rates and a grant from Government. The total income 
of the Municipality in 1912-18 was over 70,000. 
The rates are heavier than in any other town of the 
province tajiii^thsi, incidence per head of direct taxation 
excluding the taxes assessed on Government buildings 
was- Hs. 3-7-7 in 1912-13. Details with regard to the 
income and expenditure of the Municipality in 1912-13 
will he found in table XI. 

The total area of the town including the Cantonment 
is about 8 square miles and it is served by about 20 miles 



7 


of metalled and nearly 8 miles of unmetalled roads. 

An excellent supply of drinking water is obtained from

springs rising in the SbillOng Kange, and is distributed 
in pipes all over the town. 

CHAPTER VI. 

GEN SEAL ADMINISTEATION. 

A second Assistant was given to the Peputy Com- 
missioner in 1912 mainly for Excise work. ^ * 

In most of the W^r villages bordering oiji Sylhet Land rere- 
andin a few villages of the Nongpohj circle house-tax 
has been raised from Rs. 2 to Rs. 2-8 and Rs. 3 per 
house from 1907-1908. The total receipts in 1912-13 
amounted to Rs. 35,633. 

Revised rules for the leasing of land in Shillong 
were issued in 1908 under which buildiag sites can only 
be leased for a term of 99 years at a premium which 
is fixed in each case by the Deputy Commissioner, with 
an annual rental of 5 per cent, on the amount of the 
premium. 

The rate of revenue for raj kali lauds with the^eJa^tia 
exception of Bhoi, Nongphyllut, Narpuh, Rymbai, 
Nongkhlieh, Satpator and Sutnga circles, has been 
raised from ten annas to twelve annas a bigha for a 
period of 20 years from April 1912, The area of rajha>li 
lands on which revenue was assessed in 1912-13 was 
17,317 bighas which brought in a revenue of Rs. 12,294. 

It is estimated that the area of private, hali lands is 
double that of Government hnli lands. 

The high land rent paid by aliens for cultivating in

another Doloi’s circle was abolished from the year 1913- 
14. ^ The subjects of the Elhyrim Siem who come and 
cultivate within this subdivision have however not been 
exempted and they still pay a rent of Rs, 2 per field. 

House-tax has been raised from Rs. 2 to Rg. 2-8 
and Rs. 3 per house since 1907-08 and the assessment 
will run for 20 years from that date.

The reyenue from house tax in 1912-13 amounted 
to Es. 28,443. There are twenty Dolois and two 
Sardars who collect the reyenue at present. 

Owing to the political conditions and peculiar cir- 
cumstances obtaining in this district, the ordinary 
Excise rules and regulations which apply to the plains 
districts are not, as a rule, in force in these hills. A 
Khasi Extra Assistant Commissioner has been placed 
in charge of Excise work under the Deputy Commis- 
sioner, and efforts have been made to giye effect to the 
recommendations of the Excise Committee which sub- 
mitted its Eeport in 1910. There are at present three 
• country spirit dtops in the Municipality of Shillong. 
Two of these are situated in the territories of the Siem 
of Mylliem, who is accordingly giyen a moiety of the

reyenue accruing therefrom. The prices paid for these 
3 shops during the last 6 years have varied from 
Es. 10,700 to Es. 19,430 per annum. 

As a result of the Excise Enquiry Committee the 
manufacture and sale of country spirit has been brought 
under control all over the district and the unlicensed 
sale of country spirit within the five-mile radius of 
Shillong has been prohibited. (C.f. page 104 of the 
Gazetteer). 

In 1911-12 a license fee of Es. 6 per still was 
imposed upon all stills in the district, excepting those in 
the Shillong B mile zone and those in the Jowai 4 mile 
circle. 

In the Shillong and Jowai Town circles a license 
fee of Es. 26 and Es. 10 respectively has been imposed 
upon,, each st^. In the whole of the Sadar subdivi- 
sion outside of the Shillong circle, the license fee per 
still was doubled in 1913-14 and raised to Es. 16 
from April 1914, while in the Jowai subdivision outside 
the Town circle, the fee of Es. 6 per still continues still 
to be levied. 

In the British villages, the Shillong Town circle, 
and in the whole of the Jowai subdivision, licenses are 
issued by Government, while in the Ehasi States they

are issued by their respective chiefs who also receive

the whole of the revenue accruing therefrom. The 
number of stills in the British villages in the Khasi 
•Rillg (including the Shillong circle) has been redueocl 
from 243 in 1911 to 123 in 1918. In the Kliasi States 
ohe number has been reduced from 1105 to 897 within 
the same period. In the Jowai subdivision the number 
has been reduced from 370 to 351. 

There are now only 3 opium shops in the district, Opium, 
one at Civil Bazar, Shillong, and the other two at 
Langjut and Umkarto in the Jowai subdivision. 

The Mynser shop in the Jowai subdivision was closed 
on the 1st April 1911 and the Nongpoh shop in the 
Sadr subdivision was closed on the 1st April 1912. 

The average annual consumption of opium in 
the whole district for the last four years is about 24 
maunds. 

There is only one shop for the sale of ganja. It is Gauja. 
situated at Shillong. The ganja sold at the shop is 
obtained from Gauhati under a pass issued by the 
Deputy Commissioner, 

Traders and contractors still constitute the majority income te. 
of the assessees under the head “ other sources of iU' 
come. ” 

Public Works are entrusted to an Executive Pnbiio ■ 
Engineer assisted by five Upper and two Lower 
Subordinates. In addition to the care of the public 
buildings the Executive Engineer is concerned with 
the maintenance of the line of communications from 
Gauhati to Company ganj in Sylhet vid Shillong,

Dumpep and Mawphlang, Cherrapoonjee and Thcrria 
ghat. The Executive Engineer is also in charge of the 
bridle paths from Cherrapoonjee to Sheila, Tyrna to 
Ishamati, ShiUong to Laitlyngkot and all the driving 
roads around ShiUong. He also undertakes the main- 
tenance of the Shillong Water-Works xmderthe Shillong 
Municipality and acts as Government Inspector of the 
Motor Service between Gauhati and Shillong.

"With the exception of a few schools, the manage* 
meat of education in the district is in the hands of 
the Welsh Mission. 

In. the Jowai subdivision a great change has taken 
place during recent years, Non-Christians are not so 
conservative as they wore before. At Jowai itself 
village schools are attended by more than a hundred 
Non-Christian children, a thing undreamt of even during 
the last decade. Since May 1909 the inspecting staff 
has consisted of three Sub-Inspectors — one for the 
Jaintia and two for the Khasi Hills. A post of Deputy 
Inspector has also recently been added. No loss than 
12 Khasis.have up to 1913 taken the degree of Bachelor 
of Arts, of whom one passed with honours in 1898, 
another with distinction in 1913, another stood first in 
1912 in Philosophy in the Calcutta Dnivorsity and 
another took the B. L, degree in 191 2. One Khasi took 
the B. So. degree in 1913, and another passed the
